summary: This RFC specifies an RTP payload format for the FEC repair data produced by Raptor FEC Schemes, which is needed when RTP carries the repair flows in the IETF FEC Framework.

eli5.summary: It says how to pack the spare puzzle pieces into the delivery boxes used for live audio and video.

subtitle: How to carry Raptor FEC repair data in RTP for real-time media

tldr.problem: The FEC Framework and Raptor FEC Schemes work with any transport, but when repair data is carried over RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) for live video and audio, it needs a specific payload format that fits into RTP's structure.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines how to encapsulate Raptor and RaptorQ repair symbols as RTP payloads. It specifies how to use RTP headers (setting the marker bit for the last repair packet in a block, choosing timestamp rates), and registers media types for video, audio, text, and application streams.
tldr.outcome: Raptor repair flows can now be sent over RTP alongside source streams, enabling live video and audio to use Raptor FEC protection. The media type registrations allow negotiation via SDP (Session Description Protocol).

today: RFC 6682 is a Proposed Standard that defines how Raptor FEC repair flows are carried over RTP. It remains actively used in real-time media applications where packet loss protection is essential, particularly in live video streaming, video conferencing, and multicast audio/video delivery.

sections.title: RTP and FEC: Carrying Repair Data in Real Time
sections.content:
The FEC Framework (RFC 6363) defines how to send FEC repair data for any packet flow. Repair data can travel over plain UDP or over RTP.

For UDP transport, the Raptor FEC Schemes (RFC 6681) specify the exact format, and repair packets are sent directly in UDP datagrams.

For RTP transport, used for real-time media like video and audio, the repair data must be wrapped in RTP headers and follow RTP timing rules. This document specifies the RTP payload format, enabling repair flows to be sent as separate RTP streams alongside the source stream.

The advantage of RTP transport is that the repair stream can be integrated into real-time media sessions using SDP negotiation and RTCP (RTP Control Protocol) for timing coordination and quality feedback.
sections.eli5: Video and audio over the Internet use a special delivery system called RTP. When you want to send spare backup pieces over RTP, you have to wrap them the same way you wrap the main video or audio.

sections.title: How Raptor Repair Flows Work in RTP
sections.content:
In the FEC Framework context, a media session involves source flows (the actual media) and repair flows (the FEC redundancy). When carried over RTP:

  • The source flow carries the original media (video, audio, etc.) in RTP packets with a particular RTP payload type and synchronization source (SSRC).
  • The repair flow carries repair symbols as a separate RTP stream with its own payload type and SSRC.
  • Both streams are associated via SDP negotiation using the FEC grouping semantics (defined in RFC 5956).
  • The repair flow is configured with parameters from RFC 6681: the Raptor or RaptorQ scheme ID, maximum source block length (Kmax), symbol size (T), and a repair window (the maximum delay between source and repair packet transmission).

The receiver subscribes to both source and repair RTP sessions. If all source packets arrive undamaged, the repair flow can be ignored. If source packets are lost, the decoder uses received repair symbols along with available source symbols to reconstruct the missing data.
sections.eli5: Send the main video on one RTP stream and the backup pieces on another RTP stream. Tell the receiver which streams go together, and they can use the backups to fix any broken video pieces.

sections.title: RTP Header and Payload Structure
sections.content:
Raptor repair packets in RTP consist of an RTP header followed by payload data as defined in RFC 6681.

RTP Header fields:

  • Marker bit (M): Set to 1 for the last repair packet sent for each source block; otherwise 0. This signals to the receiver when a complete block of repair packets has been sent and decoding may be attempted.
  • Payload Type (PT): Assigned dynamically through SDP. Different Raptor FEC Schemes can use different payload types.
  • Timestamp: The RTP timestamp reflects when the repair packet is sent (not when the source block was sent). The timestamp rate (clock rate in Hz) is specified via the SDP media type parameter and should be at least 1000 Hz for adequate RTCP timing resolution. It is RECOMMENDED that the timestamp rate match the source stream's rate (e.g., 90 kHz for video).
  • SSRC: Must be different from the source stream's SSRC. The repair stream has its own synchronization source identifier.

Payload: Contains the Repair FEC Payload ID (as defined in RFC 6681) followed by encoded repair symbols. There is no additional payload header; the RFC 6681 Repair FEC Payload ID serves this purpose.
sections.eli5: Each backup piece has a timestamp so the receiver knows when it was sent, a flag on the last backup piece in the batch, and the original RFC 6681 information about which source block it protects.

sections.title: Media Type Registration and Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC registers four new media types for RTP use:

  • application/raptorfec — for generic FEC repair flows unrelated to a specific media type.
  • video/raptorfec — for repair flows protecting video.
  • audio/raptorfec — for repair flows protecting audio.
  • text/raptorfec — for repair flows protecting text or other time-based data.

Each media type requires four parameters:

  • rate — the RTP timestamp clock rate in Hz.
  • raptor-scheme-id — the FEC Scheme ID from RFC 6681 (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6).
  • Kmax — the Maximum Source Block Length.
  • T — the encoding symbol size in octets.
  • repair-window — the maximum time (in microseconds) between the first source packet and the last repair packet of a block.

One optional parameter:

  • P — the Payload ID format (A or B). Defaults to A if omitted.

All parameters are required except P, which is optional. They are negotiated via SDP using the a=fmtp attribute.
sections.eli5: You tell SDP which scheme you are using, how big the blocks are, how big each symbol is, and how long you wait before trying to decode. These settings are in a standard format that video and audio calls can negotiate.

sections.title: SDP Negotiation and Session Setup
sections.content:
When deploying Raptor FEC over RTP, the source and repair flows must be coordinated via SDP. The SDP offer/answer model (RFC 3264) is used to negotiate which repair scheme to use.

Key negotiation rules:

  • Each combination of Kmax and T produces different FEC data and is not compatible with others. An offerer can propose multiple configurations with different parameter sets; the answerer should select the one with the largest Kmax × T product that it supports (offering the best protection).
  • The repair window directly impacts receiver buffering requirements. Large repair windows reduce redundancy overhead but require more buffering.
  • When the P parameter is omitted, Payload ID format A is assumed.

Declarative SDP usage: In declarative modes (RTSP, SAP), the configuration is fixed and not negotiated. Multiple configurations can be offered; receivers choose the best fit.

The source and repair flows are associated using the FEC-FR (FEC Framework Repair) grouping semantics. Example:

a=group:FEC-FR S1 R1

This groups source flow S1 and repair flow R1 as a protected pair.
sections.eli5: During negotiation, you agree on which Raptor scheme to use and what parameters. Bigger blocks = less overhead but more buffering. The repair and source streams are linked by name so the receiver knows they go together.

sections.title: Repair Packet Construction and Source Recovery
sections.content:
Sending repair packets: The sender constructs repair packets by concatenating an RTP header (Section 4.1 of this RFC) with payload data (Section 4.3). The payload data contains a Repair FEC Payload ID (from RFC 6681) and repair symbols. The sender sets the marker bit to 1 on the last repair packet for each source block. Repair packet construction follows the RFC 6363 Sender Operation for RTP repair flows.

Receiving and decoding: The receiver collects RTP repair packets and associates them with their source block. When enough repair and/or source symbols have been received for a source block, the receiver invokes the FEC decoder. For Raptor codes (RFC 5053), the Example FEC Decoder in Section 5.5 may be used. For RaptorQ codes (RFC 6330), the Example FEC Decoder in Section 5.4 may be used.

RTCP coordination: RTCP (RTP Control Protocol) SHALL be used according to RFC 3550. If the repair flow is a separate RTP session from the source, both MUST be associated using the RTCP CNAME (Canonical Name), allowing synchronized timing and jitter calculations across both streams.
sections.eli5: The sender packs repair symbols with RTP headers and marks the last one. The receiver collects them and, if source packets are missing, runs the FEC decoder to rebuild the missing pieces using RFC 6681 procedures.
